title: One MCP config for Claude Code, OpenCode and OMP
summary: Developers using multiple tools (Claude Code, OpenCode, OMP) must configure MCP servers separately in different files, creating maintenance burden and authentication friction. Ivar, a new configuration manager, unifies server setup and authentication workflows across all three tools.

Three files for one server


You use Claude Code for one task and OpenCode for another, and both should see the same Figma and Linear MCP servers. Each harness wants them in its own file, under its own keys:

Writing three files once is tedious. Keeping them equal is the real cost: change a URL in one, forget the others, and half your sessions start without the server. Then each harness needs its own login.
The files are the easy part. Authentication fails differently in each harness:



server

the harness's own login

Where the harness's own login works, ivar uses it. It only takes over where the harness cannot finish. Figma MCP on OpenCode: fix "Authentication failed" explains the Figma case in detail.
Install ivar, create a hall in an empty directory with the harnesses you use, and add the servers:
curl -fsSL 'https://ivar.run/install?ref=one-mcp-config' | sh
mkdir tools-hall && cd tools-hall
ivar init --provider claude-code
ivar provider add opencode
ivar provider add omp
ivar mcp add figma
ivar mcp add linear

figma and linear are known names, so ivar mcp add fills in their URLs. Any other HTTP server takes --url, for example ivar mcp add sentry --url https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp. Adding a server that is already declared the same way changes nothing; adding one with the same name and a different URL is

title: Node.js API Routes and Server Actions: 3 Error Tracking Boundaries (With Attribution)
summary: Effective error tracking requires a stable application contract capturing both exception details and cost-attribution context (release, environment, pricing rule, cost center) before choosing an error backend. This decouples pricing logic from monitoring provider changes while maintaining support team usability.
content:
Instrument three server-side boundaries, but define the cost-attribution record before choosing the error backend. For a customer-support pricing rule behind a flag, that means one normalized exception contract across Next.js route handlers, server actions, and background jobs, with release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter attached at capture time.
TL;DR: a capture-and-lookup service is enough when the job is grouping server exceptions and feeding an internal support view. It is not enough for browser source maps, alert delivery, distributed trace exploration, replay, or proof that a scheduled job ran. Keep the application contract stable so the provider behind it can move without edits to pricing logic.
Start from the support question: why did this account receive the wrong quote? A stack trace locates the failed code. It does not identify the rule, deployment, environment, or owning budget. Those are application facts, so the application has to supply them.
I would keep eight fields. Four describe the exception: name, message, stack, and occurredAt. Four make it actionable: release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter. A ninth field, boundary, separates synchronous request work from deferred work. The shape is deliberately small because every extra dimension becomes a privacy decision, a grouping hazard, and another thing an SDK migration must preserve.
Headers need even less enthusiasm. Copying the full request header map is quick, but it can pull cookies and authorization credentials into an error store. For this workflow, allowlist content-type, user-agent, and x-request-id. Three headers. No clever redaction regex.
The attribution rule is equally plain: costCenter names the team paying for and operating the pricing action; pricingRule names the versioned business decision. Neither field should be derived from an exception message. Messages change. Identifiers should not.
That gives the support UI a useful join key without pretending an error even

title: Lock GitHub Actions dependencies to reviewed commits with workflow lockfiles
summary: GitHub Actions Workflow Lockfiles, now in public preview, pin exact commits for direct, transitive, and reusable workflow dependencies, closing the gap between code review and actual execution. The feature eliminates risks from tag movement and maintains a single source of truth for dependency versions.
content:
A moving tag is not a review


Your workflow can keep saying uses: vendor/build-action@v3 while the code behind v3 changes. That leaves a gap between the commit your team reviewed and the commit a later workflow run actually executes. Pinning every action by hand to a full commit SHA narrows that gap, but it is easy to miss transitive dependencies and reusable workflow calls.
GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles are now in public preview for Free, Team, and eligible Enterprise Cloud plans. The GitHub CLI extension gh actions-lock generates .github/workflows/actions.lock; GitHub says an onboarded workflow must have its dependencies represented there, and runs use the recorded commits even if a tag or branch moves. The file records direct actions, transitive action dependencies, and reusable-workflow dependencies. GitHub’s October 14 announcement also describes gradual onboarding, stale-lock checks, policy enforcement, and Dependabot updates. The preview is useful for teams whose review process already depends on knowing exactly what automation code will run, but a lockfile does not tell you whether the locked code is trustworthy. GitHub’s announcement explains the current preview scope and behavior.
A workflow reference such as owner/action@v3 is readable, but a tag is a name that can be moved. A full commit SHA in the workflow pins that one reference directly. The lockfile takes a different approach: your workflow can retain a human-meaningful ref while the generated lock records the exact commit to use. For an onboarded workflow, GitHub requires the needed lock entries and executes the locked commit.
That is most valuable when a workflow uses more than one action or when actions themselves call other actions. The lockfile captures those transitive dependencies too, so your review can see the resolved set rather than relying on each top-level action tag. Reusable workflows need attention as well: a reusable workflow is covered by the lockfile in the reposito

title: Title: Small projects still teach me the most
summary: Small side projects reveal real-world usability problems tutorials cannot teach—awkward mobile interactions, confusing instructions, unexpected feature usage. Launching early and iterating on friction points often delivers more value than adding new features.
content:
I like building small web projects. Sometimes it’s a game, sometimes a tool, sometimes just an idea I want to try over a weekend.
The first version is usually the easy part. The interesting problems show up later: a button that feels awkward on mobile, instructions that make sense only to me, or someone using a feature in a way I never expected.
Those details have changed how I build. I try to get something usable out early, watch where people get stuck, and fix one thing at a time. I still get tempted to add more features, but often a clearer sentence or one fewer step helps more.
I’m planning to share some of those small lessons here as I go.

title: OpenAI Decisions API: A Practical Developer's Guide
summary: OpenAI's Decisions API solves the problem of parsing vague LLM responses by returning typed verdicts instead: probabilities for yes/no questions, ranked choices for multiple-option decisions, and weighted scores for rubrics. Currently in public beta with general availability expected within weeks.
content:
If your app asks a large language model a yes-or-no question, you have probably lived through this: you request a clean label, the model replies with a paragraph, and somewhere in your codebase a regular expression tries to drag the word "refund" out of "I believe this does constitute a refund request." It works on Monday. By Friday the model is feeling chatty, the regex misses, and a support ticket goes to the wrong queue.
On 6 October, OpenAI put a public beta of a different answer in front of developers: the Decisions API, a new endpoint — POST /v1/decisions — that returns typed verdicts instead of prose. No paragraphs to parse, no JSON mode to coax, just a probability, a choice, or a score. This is a practical guide: what the endpoint does, what it costs, where it genuinely helps, and the calibration work it quietly leaves to you.
The idea is deliberately narrow. You send evidence (input) plus one or more questions, and the API answers each question in a fixed shape. Three question types exist:
Predicate — a yes-or-no condition, answered with a probability between 0 and 1. "Does this photo show visible product damage?"


Choice — a fixed set of candidate answers you define, answered with the winning choice, the option probabilities and a confidence value. "Which department owns this ticket?"


Score — an ordered rubric you define, answered with a probability-weighted average across the levels, plus a confidence. "How severe is this incident?"



A refusal is a separate answer type — not a low score and not your fallback category. As of mid-October the API is in public beta, with gpt-6-luna as the only supported model, and OpenAI says it expects general availability "in the coming weeks". That is an expectation, not a date.
The quickest way to feel the shape of the API is a support-routing call. With curl:
curl https://api.openai.com/v1/decisions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-6-l

title: How to Capture Tribal Knowledge Before You Need It: A Register, a Backup Person, and a 20-Minute Interview
summary: Organizational tribal knowledge—procedures known to only one person—can be systematically discovered through targeted 15-minute interviews, tracked in a spreadsheet with backup-person and documentation status, and prioritized by coverage gaps. A formula-driven status tracker highlights single points of failure and outdated procedures.
content:
This article is AI-generated.
Every team has things that only one or two people know. How to restart the label printer when it jams. Which customer needs certificates in a particular format. Why a step in the month-end process is done in that odd order. None of it is written down because it never seemed worth writing down, until the person who knows is on holiday, off sick, or gone.
The usual advice is "document everything," which is why it rarely happens. This guide takes a narrower approach: find out what only one person knows, decide which of it matters, and capture it in short, repeatable sessions.
Tribal knowledge is hard to list because people don't notice they have it. Instead of asking "what do you know?", ask questions that surface it:
"What do people come to you for that they can't get anywhere else?"
"If you were away for two weeks, what would go wrong first?"
"What do you do that isn't in any procedure?"
"Which questions do new starters ask you most often?"
Ask these of each team member in a 15-minute conversation. Write each answer as a short topic, for example "Restarting label printer after jam" or "Certificate format for customer X."

title: I Burned 95% of My AI Coding Quota in 2 Days — Here's What the Logs Revealed
summary: Analysis of three days of Claude Code usage revealed 99.9% of tokens were context re-reads and 97.6% were cached material; long sessions with growing context and parallel subagents amplified token costs dramatically. Breaking work into focused sessions, reducing parallel review cycles, and using smaller models for routine tasks can cut consumption by 75%.
content:
I use Claude Code every day to build a SaaS product. This week, the usage meter hit 95% before Wednesday. I assumed I had somehow written a mountain of code.
I hadn't.
Every request is logged locally, so I added it up. Here's what three days of work looked like (October 12–15):
65,000 requests
12.6 billion tokens processed
14 million tokens of actual output
That means 99.9% of my tokens weren't code. They were the model re-reading what it already knew.
97.6% of all tokens were cache reads. Every turn, the agent resends the entire conversation so far: files read, tool results, earlier decisions.
When the context sits at 200k tokens, a one-line reply still costs 200k tokens of reading.
Two thirds of my volume came from requests with more than 200k tokens of context. Only 2.5% came from requests under 50k.
A long session doesn't cost more because it does more. It costs more because every new turn is more expensive than the last.
My workflow splits work into small tasks. For each task, one subagent implements and two review — one for spec conformance, one for code quality. It produces clean results.
It also produced 78% of my requests and 53% of my tokens.
Each subagent starts with a fresh but still large context, runs many tool calls, and each call re-reads that context. One task becomes dozens of requests.
Out of 46 sessions, five accounted for three quarters of the total volume. These were multi-hour runs where the context kept growing and I never started over. One of them averaged almost 400k tokens of context per request.

The certification checks that you can run a Cortex XDR console as a SOC analyst: triage alerts, investigate incidents, query data and manage endpoint policy. It sits at the Specialist level in the Security Operations track, according to the XDR Analyst certification page.
You book the exam through Pearson VUE, and Palo Alto delivers it in English worldwide. The blueprint is short enough to print on one page, and every task in it is numbered, which makes it easy to tick off as you study.

title: Understanding Solar Street Light Installation Layouts
summary: Solar street light installation requires choosing between single-side, double-side (opposite or staggered), center-median, and cable-suspension arrangements, each suited to different road geometries and coverage requirements. The appropriate layout depends on road width, pole height, and desired lighting uniformity rather than any universal optimal configuration.
content:
Solar street light installation is not just about choosing a suitable lamp and mounting it on a pole. The arrangement of the lights along a road also affects lighting coverage, uniformity, and the overall design of a project.
Several common layouts are used in road lighting. Each has different requirements depending on road width, pole height, available space, and the desired lighting distribution.

Single-Side Arrangement
In a single-side arrangement, all light poles are installed along one side of the road.
This layout is often considered for narrow roads, access roads, and smaller streets where one-sided installation can provide sufficient coverage. However, the road width, mounting height, and light distribution must be evaluated carefully to avoid uneven illumination on the opposite side.
Double-Side Arrangement
Double-side arrangements place poles along both sides of the road. Two common configurations are used.
Opposite arrangement: Poles on both sides face each other at similar positions. This can provide a more balanced lighting pattern across the road.
Staggered arrangement: Poles alternate between the two sides rather than lining up directly opposite each other. This may help distribute light more evenly along the road, depending on the luminaire's optical design and pole spacing.
Neither configuration is automatically better. The appropriate choice depends on the road geometry and the required lighting performance.
Center Arrangement
In a center arrangement, light poles are installed along the central divider or median of a road, with luminaires positioned to illuminate the required areas on either side.
This layout may be suitable for divided roads and wider road sections where a central installation is practical. Pole structure, mounting height, and luminaire orientation must be designed to provide adequate coverage in both directions.

zh.title: 理解太阳能路灯安装布局
zh.summary: 太阳能路灯安装需要在单侧、双侧（相对或交错）、中央分隔带和电缆悬挂等布局中进行选择，每种布局适合不同的道路几何形状和覆盖要求。合适的布局取决于道路宽度、杆高和所需的照明均匀性，而不是任何通用的最优配置。
